     "subtitle": "From clinical dietitian to triathlete: Who is Luka Batur and how does he combine science with the field?",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur in the studio explains the importance of knowing biochemistry and human metabolism in sports nutrition.",
     "content": "In a new episode of the podcast on the *biciklizam_net* channel, host Josip welcomed Luka Batur, a Master of Nutrition for whom this is already his third appearance on the show. The occasion for the conversation is the publication of the most comprehensive scientific review of nutrition in professional cycling, which dissects the period from 2016 to 2025, and along with that, Batur's authored guide to cyclist nutrition was also presented, in which he covers the role of macronutrients and strategies for food intake before, during, and after a ride.\n\nTo bring his professional credibility closer to the viewers, Luka Batur points out that behind him is not just a weekend course, but a graduate study at the Faculty of Food Technology and Biotechnology of the University of Zagreb, which he completed in 2021. The foundation of his work consists of a deep knowledge of chemistry, biochemistry, and human metabolism, which he considers the key difference between true scientists and self-proclaimed experts who build their authority exclusively on the fact that they have been riding a bicycle for a long time. After university, he got a job at KBC Zagreb as a clinical dietitian, where he still works today with patients with various medical diagnoses, while simultaneously conducting consultations for amateur and professional athletes.\n\nWhat sets Batur apart in practice is the fact that he himself has been actively training for triathlon since 2017, thereby understanding the demands of cycling firsthand. He emphasizes that since graduating, the scientific facts themselves have not changed drastically, but he himself has progressed significantly in his approach to clients and in shaping dry data into something that is truly achievable for people in the field. He regularly upgrades his knowledge at international professional gatherings, such as the big congress in Manchester that he visited two years ago with a fellow nutritionist, where he listened live to the world's leading names in sports nutrition who stand precisely behind the new series of papers on cycling.",

     "subtitle": "Secrets of professional teams and marginal gains: What do scientists keep from the competition?",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur talks about the secrets of professional cycling teams and the role of scientists in achieving marginal gains.",
     "content": "Entering the topic of professional cycling, host Josip notes how the stigma of doping is historically tied to this sport, but today the key advantage over the competition – the so-called *marginal gains* – is created through legal micro-details in nutrition. Since all top teams today ride equally perfect bicycles and train according to similar principles, specific nutritional strategies are becoming the decisive factor.\n\nLuka Batur agrees that the main stars of sports nutrition in professional teams certainly do not reveal all their secrets to the public. Scientific papers published today are often the result of research conducted up to two years earlier. In the meantime, top teams conduct internal analyses in their laboratories, such as muscle biopsies of their riders, and keep every new revolutionary discovery exclusively for themselves as long as it brings them a competitive advantage. Batur compares this to hiding power data (watts) on the Strava platform during races like the Tour de France.\n\nAs an example of a top combination of science and practice, Batur singles out scientists who are athletes themselves and who in university laboratories literally discovered the today generally accepted standards on the intake of 60 to 90 grams of carbohydrates through a combination of glucose and fructose. Such experts were at the beginning even frustrated by how slowly their scientific findings actually reach coaches and riders in the field itself.",

     "subtitle": "The new 'Bible' of cycling: How is scientific consensus formed through heated debates?",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur recounts an anecdote from a congress about heated scientific debates among the world's leading nutritionists.",
     "content": "The comprehensive scientific review commissioned by the International Cycling Union (UCI) actually consists of a series of six to seven connected papers that are completely open to the public (*open access*). Luka Batur states that behind these papers stands the absolute cream of world nutrition: experts who led nutrition in teams such as Jumbo-Visma, Bora-Hansgrohe, and Ineos, among whom is James Morton (also known for his work with the Liverpool football club), and the Australian scientist Louise Burke.\n\nBatur enthusiastically recounts an anecdote from the congress in Manchester that illustrates how the top scientific community functions. A year earlier, a controversial paper titled *Does RED-S exist?* was published, which questioned the existence of the syndrome of relative energy deficiency in sport (a state in which a lack of calories leads to hormonal disorders, loss of the menstrual cycle in women, and bone stress fractures). That paper caused huge problems for practitioners because athletes obsessed with weight loss used it as an excuse for starvation. At the next congress, Louise Burke held a lecture *RED-S does exist*, in which she directly and fiercely called out the authors of the mentioned paper. Despite that stormy public debate, all those scientists today again jointly sign the new UCI papers. Batur points out that such healthy constructive criticism is chronically lacking in Croatia, noting that he himself has been blocked on social media by domestic colleagues just because he pointed out the methodological shortcomings of a paper.\n\nThe value of this UCI review, as Batur explains, is not in bringing completely unknown revolutions – because glycogen and supercompensation were known back in the sixties of the last century – but in uniting all previous science in one place and supplementing it with field experience. The texts often contain the label *personal observation* (personal observations of nutritionists from Grand Tour races), thereby creating a kind of 'Bible' for experts and athletes.",

     "subtitle": "From expenditure on mountain stages to mobile kitchens: What does the UCI review reveal?",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur holds notes and explains how one of the scientific papers covers the role of chefs and mobile kitchens at races.",
     "content": "Analyzing the content of the UCI papers, host Josip looks back at the fascinating data on how average speeds at races like the Giro d'Italia have drastically increased over the years, which directly entails a huge caloric expenditure. Luka Batur explains that the series of papers covers absolutely every aspect of the life and work of a professional cyclist. Nutrition periodization is covered in detail, not only during the approximately 80 competitive days in a year (when riders complete two Grand Tours and a few classics), but also through the remaining 250 training days and in the off-season period.\n\nIn the papers, the needs on the stages themselves are precisely dissected, whereby the myth that professionals intake the famous 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour every single day is shattered. On shorter and flatter stages, intake drops to 50 grams per hour, while extreme numbers remain reserved for difficult mountain stages (*mountain stages*) that last six hours each with thousands of meters of elevation gain.\n\nThe review also encompasses the following key units:\n- **Recovery and injury prevention:** The focus is not only on recovery immediately after one training session, but on long-term preservation of health from day to day and from month to month.\n- **Supplementation and sports food (*sports food*):** A clear division of dietary supplements into those that are proven to work, those that are useless, and those that are potentially dangerous, with practical comparisons of gels and energy bars.\n- **From plate to performance (*From plate to performance*):** A special paper written by two female authors deals exclusively with logistics in the kitchen. It describes how club nutritionists cooperate with professional cooks (*chefs*) in restaurants and special team trucks with mobile kitchens, whose task is to turn dry tables and gram weights into tasty and digestible meals on a plate.\n\nAt the mention of mobile kitchens, Josip shared a funny personal anecdote from preparations on Rogla, where he came across the trucks and buses of the Jumbo-Visma team. When the lenses of his sunglasses fell out of the frame, he asked the staff for help so he could safely descend from the mountain, but they misunderstood him, thinking that he was begging them for free glasses, and rejected him quite coldly.",

     "subtitle": "The myth of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour: Why shouldn't recreational riders copy professionals?",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur warns recreational riders that an intake of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour does not automatically guarantee a better result at the finish.",
     "content": "One of the biggest misconceptions in modern amateur sport is blindly copying professional cyclists and triathletes. Luka Batur points out how recreational riders often see that top professionals intake 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour, so they try to do the same on an indoor trainer in a ride of only an hour and fifteen minutes or on an easy Sunday group ride. To understand why this is wrong, Batur brings the story back to the basics of physiology: carbohydrates are 'rocket fuel' for our muscles, and their intake is exclusively dictated by the **intensity** and **volume** of the activity.\n\nOn a typical weekend ride of a hundred kilometers in a group of about twenty cyclists, most riders spend most of the time in the slipstream, in easy Zone 2, with an average power of only 150 watts. In such conditions, glycogen expenditure is not extreme and it makes no sense at all to burden the digestive system with 120 grams of sugar per hour. Batur emphasizes the key message of the UCI paper itself: a higher intake of carbohydrates does not automatically mean a faster entry into the finish line. On the other hand, the positive thing is that this trend has at least encouraged amateurs to eat more than before, since recreational riders used to – just like riders at the Tour de France a few decades ago – intake only 0 to 30 grams per hour.\n\nFor 80 to 90 percent of more serious recreational riders who ride three to five times a week, having two more intense rides of two and a half to three and a half hours, it is quite enough to stick to an intake of **60 grams per hour**, or raise it toward **80 or 90 grams** only when the intensity is truly high. Professionals can spend huge amounts of fuel because they are able to maintain work for hours at 80 to 90 percent of their maximum oxygen uptake (VO2 max) and keep their heart rate at 175 or 180 beats per minute, which an average recreational rider physiologically simply cannot perform.\n\nAnswering Josip's question on how complete recreational riders who ride long *brevets* without competitive pressure should position themselves toward food, Batur offers a very simple analogy with a car. If you drive locally with a little fuel on reserve, you will get home without a problem; but if you are rushing down the highway to Dubrovnik at a speed of 150 km/h, you must precisely plan every stop at a gas station. Therefore, on a relaxed *brevet* one does not need to add up grams with a pencil on paper, but it is crucial to eat continuously – roughly one energy bar or gel per hour with a little sweetened liquid in the bottle – so that the ride remains a pleasure. Josip confirmed this with his own bad experience from a difficult ride across Žumberak, when he ate nothing for the first two and a half hours, saving food for later, only to suddenly eat a sandwich, a heavy energy bar, and gummy candies at the top of the climb, which resulted in a complete stomach blockage, nausea, and a drop in energy.",

     "subtitle": "Gels, bars, or solid food: What and when to eat during a ride?",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur explains why in race conditions one should avoid fats, proteins, and fiber in energy bars.",
     "content": "The choice between liquid food, gels, and energy bars during a cycling ride directly depends on the intensity of the effort and the configuration of the terrain. Nutritionist **Luka Batur** points out that at high intensity, for example during a fast group ride in a peloton when the heart rate reaches 170 beats per minute, it becomes extremely difficult and impractical to chew solid food. In such situations, liquid and gels are the absolute priority. On the other hand, energy bars and solid food are reserved for calmer parts of the route, whereby it is important to know the course profile so that solid food is not consumed immediately at the beginning of a demanding climb.\n\nWhen it comes to the composition of solid food during intense training sessions or races, science is very clear. Batur emphasizes that such bars must contain:\n- **As little fat as possible**\n- **As little protein as possible**\n- **As little fiber as possible**\n\nThe goal is for solid food in those conditions to be almost pure carbohydrate. The reason lies in the physiology of digestion: fats, proteins, and fiber slow down gastric emptying and the transit of glucose and food from the stomach into the intestines, and then from the intestines into the bloodstream. In race conditions, the primary goal is for the fuel to reach the muscles from the blood as quickly as possible. Because of this, Batur does not recommend protein bars to anyone during the rides and races themselves, because proteins are not a significant source of energy on a bicycle, while for preserving muscle mass, the total daily intake after the end of the activity is decisive anyway. With relaxed *coffee ride* rides without high intensity, the rules are significantly more flexible and recreational riders can choose what is tasty to them.\n\nLooking back at the previous experience of host **Josip**, who on one ride ate nothing for the first two and a half hours and then caused a blockage in his stomach with a sudden intake of food, Batur warns that delaying food intake is a big mistake. As the training or race progresses, the body becomes more and more tired, and most of the blood is directed into the working muscles and extremities which require oxygen and nutrients during great efforts. Consequently, the digestive system and stomach have a weaker blood supply, which results in poorer contractions, mixing, and the digestion of food itself. Therefore, it is crucial to start with food intake as early as possible, while the body is not yet under stress, in order to utilize the maximum functionality of the digestive system and avoid digestive troubles. Batur states that on targeted hard rides and races, thanks to the trained state of his gut, he takes his first gel already after 15 to 20 minutes of riding.",

     "subtitle": "Physiology of the gut and how the number of 120 grams of carbohydrates was reached",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur talks about glucose and fructose transporters and limitations at the gut level.",
     "content": "To Josip's question about how scientists even arrived at the famous number of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour, Luka Batur explains the methodology of laboratory research, the kind that colleagues in **Ljubljana** also conduct today. In these tests, a carbohydrate solution is labeled with special isotopes, after which the athlete drinks it, and scientists use masks and indirect calorimetry to measure the amount of exhaled carbon dioxide ($CO_2$). Based on the difference between the ingested and exhaled isotope, it is precisely calculated how much glucose the body has spent.\n\nSearching for where the physiological barrier of usability is located exactly, in one experiment in the laboratory, scientists gave cyclists a direct infusion of glucose into the bloodstream. It turned out that almost all glucose that is directly injected into the blood enters the cells without a problem and is spent in the muscles during pedaling. This led to a key conclusion: the limitation is not in the muscles themselves, rather the barrier is located in the digestive system, more precisely at the level of the intestines.\n\nBatur vividly compares this mechanism to toll booths on a highway. In the intestines, there are specific receptors, and glucose enters through a transporter named **SGLT1** (*sodium-glucose transporter 1*). Research with labeled isotopes showed that the maximum capacity of that transporter for glucose is around 60 grams per hour. However, it was subsequently discovered that fructose uses completely different transporters in the intestines. By combining glucose and fructose, passage through both \"booths\" simultaneously is enabled, whereby the total absorption of carbohydrates can be raised to significantly higher levels and thus deliver additional fuel into the bloodstream.",

     "subtitle": "Alternatives to expensive gels: Regular sugar, glucose, and honey",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur answers viewers' questions about using regular sugar, store-bought glucose, and honey.",
     "content": "Answering viewers' questions about cheaper replacements for expensive commercial gels and sports drinks – such as regular white sugar (sucrose), which naturally contains a 50:50 ratio of glucose and fructose with the addition of a little salt, or honey – Luka Batur points out that buying expensive gels is truly not necessary. Scientific research has compared different types of sugar, including pure glucose, fructose, and even lactose.\n\nAlthough table white sugar (sucrose) is a usable option, Batur still gives a slight advantage to pure glucose (dextrose) or maltodextrin from specialized stores. The reason lies in the physical properties of sugar, because sucrose and fructose can cause greater chaos in the intestines in some individuals, while pure glucose is better tolerated and creates less digestive stress. Batur also recalled his own student days when, due to a limited budget, he did not buy expensive products, but bought pure glucose in **dm** stores and mixed it independently.\n\nWhen it comes to honey, Batur states that he has never used it as a replacement for gels, primarily due to the high price and logistical impracticality when carrying and squeezing it during the ride itself. For recreational rides that do not have a competitive character, regular gummy candies are also an excellent and affordable alternative. As a practical conclusion, Batur emphasizes that at lower carbohydrate intakes – up to 60 grams per hour – the exact ratios of glucose and fructose and the sources themselves are significantly less important. Josip follows up with the conclusion that the main advantage of commercial gels is the practicality of the packaging and fast absorption at races, while for recreational riders they can serve only as \"first aid\" in the pocket, noting that viewers can get products of the **4Endurance** brand with a discount.",

     "subtitle": "Injury prevention through nutrition and the dangers of energy deficiency (RED-S)",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur explains the syndrome of relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) and its consequences on bones and hormones.",
     "content": "One of the rarely mentioned, yet extremely important topics in sports nutrition is injury prevention through nutrition. While Josip notes how laypeople mostly associate injury prevention with stretching, warming up, and the gym, Luka Batur explains that in scientific papers this concept primarily refers to avoiding the syndrome of relative energy deficiency in sport, known as **RED-S** (*Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport*).\n\nIn practice, Batur often encounters male athletes, and especially female athletes, who are preoccupied with body mass and appearance and train for weeks or months in a serious, unstructured energy deficit without the supervision of an expert. Such chronic deprivation of calories leaves severe consequences on the organism:\n- **In women:** The first alarm sign is the loss of the menstrual cycle, which indicates that the body is shutting down functions that at that moment are not essential for survival. Due to hormonal disorders, bones become porous and hollow, so even young girls of 20 years of age can bring themselves into a state of osteopenia.\n- **In men:** Chronic energy deficit is reflected through a drop in testosterone levels and a general drop in vitality.\n- **General risks:** Athletes in a deficit complete training sessions significantly worse, are more susceptible to infections due to a drop in immunity, and in the event of a fall from a bicycle, they have significantly higher chances for severe bone fractures.\n\nThe authors of the review paper therefore clearly point out that supplements like calcium and vitamin D are always in the background compared to ensuring an adequate intake of energy. In multi-day intense efforts, the primary goal is to minimize the energy deficit and compensate for what was spent. At the same time, Batur warns of a frequent mistake by amateurs who copy professionals during training, and even eat a quality meal immediately after a ride, but completely neglect nutrition for the rest of the day. For a five-hour training session, recommendations reach up to 10 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body mass daily, which is a huge amount of food that athletes often do not intake because they spend the rest of the day on fast food and beer. Josip confirms this with his own experience when, combining cycling and the gym, he was in a weekly deficit of 3500 to 5000 calories, skimping on carbohydrates due to the influence of the fitness industry, which led him to chronic fatigue.",

     "subtitle": "Case study: Luka Batur's nutrition before, during, and after a Granfondo",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur describes his race day menu in detail, including breakfast, caffeine intake, and the amount of gels.",
     "content": "To bring theory closer to practice, Josip and Luka Batur analyzed Batur's own nutrition before, during, and after a recent Sunday **Granfondo** race, which he finished in two hours and 42 minutes. When it comes to filling glycogen stores (supercompensation), scientific papers show that stores can be filled already within 24 hours before the race, although in practice it is often more pleasant to distribute this over two days to avoid overeating. Theoretical recommendations for maximum loading amount to around 10 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body mass, which for Batur, who is close to 90 kilograms, would mean almost a kilogram of pure carbohydrates.\n\nHis protocol for this race looked like this:\n- **The day before the race (Saturday):** The focus was on a high intake of carbohydrates while avoiding fats and fiber. He ate a whole 400-gram package of apple and cherry strudels from **Spar**, half a package of pasta (which he shared with his girlfriend), a large portion of **Čokolino**, a lot of fruit, a jam sandwich, and a package of 8 to 10 *Jaffa* cakes. In order not to burden his digestion with too large a volume of solid food, he replaced a large part of water with liquid calories like **Cedevita** and juices.\n- **The morning before the race (Sunday):** Since the race started at 10:45 AM, he had an early breakfast of a large portion of Čokolino with *low-fat* milk with the addition of **Kraš Express** and a piece of cake. He also took in a large amount of caffeine – around half a liter of coffee – and half an hour before the start he ate a handful of gummy candies and drank a three-deciliter can of **Red Bull**.\n- **During the race:** In two bottles (one of 0.7 l and the other of 0.5 l) he had a total of around 120 grams of carbohydrates from isotonics, at the feed zone he took another isotonic, and during the ride he ate 5 of the 6 gels he brought. In total, in 2 hours and 42 minutes he took in around 200 grams of carbohydrates, which proved to be quite enough, despite cramps in the last few kilometers which were the consequence of a strong pace.\n\nThe race was also marked by an anecdote with his girlfriend **Marija Lukina**, a former member of the triathlon club **Rudolf Perešin** and a previous winner of that race, who entered the finish line just a few seconds behind him, pulling along with colleague **Jadran Peran** an entire group of cyclists between the 70th and 100th place. Since it was Marija's birthday that day, and a *Half Ironman* triathlon awaited Batur already the following weekend, recovery began immediately after the finish line with a portion of *bolognese* pasta, after which he ate forest fruit in the apartment (as a replacement for tart cherry juice used by professionals), and at the celebration at her parents' place, meat with potatoes, rolls, cakes, and a birthday cake followed. Batur emphasizes that papers show how in extreme efforts sometimes not even 13 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body mass is enough for a complete renewal of glycogen within 24 hours, which is why an abundant intake of food after a race is crucial if a new challenge awaits the athlete soon.",

     "subtitle": "Maintaining muscle mass and protein intake on multi-day rides",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur explains the role of strength training and total daily protein intake in preserving muscle mass.",
     "content": "Answering the question of viewer **Marin Milardović** on how to most safely maintain muscle mass and lose exclusively fat during races or multi-day *bikepacking* tours, Luka Batur first separates the role of training from the role of nutrition. Professional cyclists have an extremely thin upper body for a reason, because a large muscle mass in that part is not in their interest. For the maintenance or growth of muscle mass itself, the primary condition is an adequate stimulus, namely strength training and lifting weights, which is the domain of kinesiologists. \"If we could influence muscles exclusively through some nutritional intervention, I think all our politicians would be bodybuilders given how much meat they eat,\" Batur comments vividly.\n\nFrom the nutritional side, the key to preserving muscles lies in an adequate total daily intake of protein, whereby the scientific consensus is that **1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body mass** daily is quite enough for maintenance, and even for muscle growth. Batur repeats that there is no scientific evidence whatsoever that protein needs to be taken in during the ride itself, even if it lasts six or seven hours, because nothing bad will happen to the muscles in that period as long as daily needs are met through breakfast before departure and dinner after the end of the ride.\n\nStill, in the specific context of multi-day *bikepacking*, where the rider spends the whole day on the bicycle and in the evening in a tent or restaurant perhaps for practical reasons cannot eat a sufficient amount of meat, fish, or eggs, consuming a protein bar during the day is completely acceptable because such a ride does not have the competitive intensity of a Granfondo. If someone goes on a one-month *bikepacking* trip across Europe, it is normal that upon returning to the gym they will notice a slight drop in strength on the *bench press* or pull-ups simply because for a month they did not provide the muscles with a specific training stimulus. However, since Josip notes that the mentioned viewer plans a *bikepacking* trip lasting only five to seven days, both conclude that in such a short period no loss of muscle mass will occur and that there is no need whatsoever to perform strength exercises at rest stops along the road.",

     "subtitle": "Nutrition on brevets and long rides and myths about magnesium",
     "screenshot_description": "Luka Batur explains why heavy food like bacon and eggs is not ideal for long cycling rides.",
     "content": "In the third part of the conversation, host Josip opens viewers' questions, starting with an inquiry from viewer Damir about nutrition before and during brevets and long rides. Damir states that on brevets cyclists eat all sorts of things, while he personally consumes sandwiches with eggs and bacon, various chocolate bars, and drinks water, so he is interested in when and how much magnesium should be taken.\n\nLuka Batur points out that the combination of eggs and bacon would never be his first choice, primarily due to the slowing down of gastric emptying. Although fats contribute to total energy expenditure, the fact is that even individuals with the lowest percentage of body fat have quite enough fat stores for the needs of training or a race. Therefore, it is a shame for fats to take the place of carbohydrates. Still, Batur notes that the brevet format is not the same as a race. If someone feels good doing it, the approach can be more relaxed than at a granfondo, but he personally would never bring a sandwich with eggs and pancetta. Instead, he advises reducing the intake of bacon and protein and switching to milder options, such as a few slices of ham or a lighter spread.\n\nAs an example from his own practice, Batur recalls his bicycle ride from Zagreb to Šibenik a few years ago, when he had only one or two bags with him. Along the way he ate two strudels, drank half a liter of Coca-Cola, and consumed bars, carbohydrates, and gummy candies. On the section from Gračac to Knin, when he was already in more serious dehydration, he was saved by three deciliters of water and a package of Kandit jelly slices. He emphasizes that he would not go on such tours with the goal of turning them into an eating competition, as if it were about a wedding or Christmas platter.\n\nWhen it comes to **magnesium**, Batur busts frequent myths circulating in recreational circles:\n- **Minimal losses through sweat:** Losses of magnesium via sweat are extremely low, almost non-existent, therefore there are no recommendations for its intake during the activity itself.\n- **Poor absorption of commercial forms:** Most magnesium bought in packets comes in poor forms like oxide or carbonate, of which the body absorbs only around three percent.\n- **Risk of digestive issues:** Taking magnesium before or during a ride can cause a laxative effect.\n\nBecause of everything stated, Batur concludes that he would not drink magnesium at all before or during a ride, rather he personally takes it exclusively in the evening, and in the form of glycinate.",
